title: Liquid I.V. for a Hangover: Does It Work? Timing and Dose
excerpt: Does Liquid I.V. help a hangover? What it fixes (dehydration) and what it can't (acetaldehyde, sleep, nausea), when to drink it, how many sticks a day, and who should skip it.
metaDescription: Does Liquid I.V. help a hangover? What it fixes and what it can't, whether to take it before or after drinking, and how many sticks a day is safe.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Liquid I.V. can help with one part of a hangover, the dehydration part. It's a reasonably well-designed oral rehydration mix, and drinking a stick in 16 ounces of water the morning after (or before bed) will rehydrate you somewhat faster than plain water. That can take the edge off thirst, dry mouth, a dehydration headache, and the lightheaded feeling when you stand up. What it can't do is touch the other causes of a hangover: the toxic by-product of alcohol called acetaldehyde, the inflammation, the broken sleep, and the irritated stomach. So expect "a bit better," not "cured."

**The quick rules:** One stick in 16 ounces of water is a sensible dose. One before bed and one in the morning is plenty for most people after a night out. Don't go past what the package suggests, and skip it or ask a doctor first if you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or you've been told to limit salt. If you can't keep any fluid down, Liquid I.V. won't fix that, and repeated vomiting is a reason to get checked.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label information. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor before using electrolyte mixes regularly if** you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, or you take medicines that affect potassium or sodium (some blood pressure pills and water pills, for example).

## Does Liquid I.V. Help a Hangover?

Yes, partly. To see why the answer is "partly," it helps to know what a hangover actually is.

A hangover isn't one problem. It's several things happening at once after your body has processed a lot of alcohol:

1. **Dehydration and fluid loss.** Alcohol makes you pee more than you drink (more on why below). You wake up short on water and some salts.
2. **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, before breaking it down further. It's linked to nausea, headache, flushing, and the general poisoned feeling.
3. **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking triggers an immune response. Researchers increasingly think this is a major driver of how lousy you feel.
4. **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but wrecks the second half of the night, so you wake up unrested even after eight hours in bed.
5. **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid, which causes nausea and heartburn.
6. **Low blood sugar, for some people.** Alcohol can interfere with how your liver releases sugar, which adds to shakiness and fatigue.

Liquid I.V. addresses number one directly and number six a little (it contains sugar). It does nothing meaningful for two through five.

Here's an important twist. When researchers have measured hydration markers and electrolytes in hungover volunteers, they've generally found only a weak link between how dehydrated people were and how bad their hangover felt. Dehydration is real after heavy drinking, and fixing it helps the thirst and dry mouth, but it isn't the main reason a hangover is miserable. That's why someone can drink a liter of water before bed and still wake up feeling terrible.

So the realistic expectation is this: Liquid I.V. is a good way to rehydrate. It is not a hangover cure, and there is no good evidence that any electrolyte drink, Liquid I.V. included, shortens or prevents a hangover on its own.

## Why Alcohol Dehydrates You in the First Place

Alcohol blocks a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone). Vasopressin's job is to tell your kidneys to hold on to water. When alcohol suppresses it, your kidneys let more water pass into your bladder, and you end up peeing more than the volume you drank. That's the familiar "breaking the seal" experience.

A few other things add to the fluid loss on a night out:

- **Sweating** in hot bars, on dance floors, or outdoors in summer.
- **Vomiting or diarrhea**, which cause much bigger losses of water, sodium, and potassium than peeing does.
- **Not drinking water** alongside the alcohol, which is the most common reason people wake up parched.

When you lose fluid this way, you also lose some sodium and potassium. That's the logic behind electrolyte drinks: replace the water and the salts together, rather than water alone.

## What's Actually in Liquid I.V.

Liquid I.V.'s main product is called Hydration Multiplier. It comes as a powder stick that you mix into 16 ounces (about 500 ml) of water. The exact numbers vary a little by flavor and change over time, so always check your box, but a standard stick of the original formula has roughly:

- **Sodium:** around 500 mg
- **Potassium:** around 370 mg
- **Sugar:** around 11 g (from cane sugar and dextrose)
- **Calories:** around 45
- **Vitamin C** and several **B vitamins** (B3, B5, B6, B12)

The brand calls its approach "Cellular Transport Technology." Strip away the marketing name and it's the same principle behind oral rehydration solutions used in medicine for decades: a specific balance of sodium and glucose helps your gut absorb water faster than water alone. Sodium and glucose are absorbed together through the intestinal wall, and water follows them. That science is solid and well established.

There are also other versions. The **Sugar-Free** line swaps most of the sugar for allulose and other sweeteners, which helps if you're watching sugar but slightly weakens the sodium-glucose effect. The brand has also sold **Energy** versions with caffeine and **Sleep** versions with melatonin and other ingredients. Those are different products with different trade-offs after drinking, covered below.

### How it compares to a medical rehydration solution

The World Health Organization's oral rehydration solution, designed for people with serious dehydration from diarrhea, contains more sodium per liter than a stick of Liquid I.V. mixed as directed, and a little less sugar. Pedialyte sits in a similar range to Liquid I.V. on sodium. Sports drinks like regular Gatorade contain much less sodium and more sugar.

What that means in practice:

| Drink | Sodium | Sugar | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Liquid I.V. (one stick in 16 oz) | High for a consumer drink | Moderate | Rehydrating after a normal night out |
| Pedialyte (classic) | Similar range | Moderate | Same job; a bit closer to a medical formula |
| Regular sports drink | Low | Higher | Exercise; weaker for rehydration |
| Plain water | None | None | Mild dehydration; always fine |
| WHO-style oral rehydration salts | Highest | Lower | Significant fluid loss from vomiting or diarrhea |

Liquid I.V. is a legitimate rehydration drink, not just flavored water. It just isn't the strongest option if you've been sick all night. For more on how the two biggest names stack up, see our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) comparison.

## What Liquid I.V. Fixes, and What It Doesn't

It's worth being specific, because this is where most disappointment comes from.

**Likely to help:**

- Thirst and dry mouth
- Lightheadedness when you stand up quickly
- A headache that's partly from dehydration
- Dark yellow urine and peeing less than usual
- A little low-energy feeling from low blood sugar (the sugar version)

**Unlikely to help:**

- Nausea driven by acetaldehyde and stomach irritation
- The heavy, foggy, inflamed feeling
- Fatigue from poor sleep
- Anxiety the next day (sometimes called hangxiety)
- Sensitivity to light and sound

If your main hangover symptom is a pounding head and a desert-dry mouth, Liquid I.V. is a reasonable first move. If your main symptom is nausea, it may even be hard to drink 16 ounces at once. Small sips work better, and our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers what to do about the stomach side.

## Liquid I.V. Before or After Drinking?

Timing matters more than most people realize. Here's how each window plays out.

### Before you go out

Drinking a stick in the afternoon before a night out starts you off well hydrated. That's not a bad idea, especially on a hot day or if you've been active. But it won't stop alcohol from making you pee, and it does nothing about acetaldehyde. Think of it as "start with a full tank," not as prevention.

### While you're drinking

Alternating alcoholic drinks with water is one of the most useful habits there is, mainly because it slows your drinking down. You can make one of those waters a Liquid I.V. if you like. Don't mix the powder into alcohol, though. Mixing it into a cocktail doesn't cancel the alcohol's effect on your kidneys, and the sweet taste can make it easier to drink more alcohol faster.

### Before bed

This is probably the single best time. A stick in 16 ounces of water before you sleep gives your body several hours to absorb the fluid and salts while alcohol is still pushing water out. If you'll be up to pee once in the night, that's a fair trade.

### The next morning

Also a good time, and the one most people use. Drink it slowly over 20 to 30 minutes rather than chugging it, especially if your stomach is unsettled. Pair it with some food, because a light breakfast helps with blood sugar and gives your stomach something besides acid to work on.

Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) goes deeper on timing for all electrolyte drinks, not just Liquid I.V.

## How Many Liquid I.V. Sticks Can You Have in a Day?

For a typical hangover, one or two sticks is enough. A common pattern is one before bed and one the next morning. Check your package for its own guidance, and don't go beyond it.

Here's why more isn't better:

- **Sodium adds up.** At roughly 500 mg a stick, three sticks is about 1,500 mg of sodium from drinks alone. US dietary guidelines suggest most adults keep total sodium under about 2,300 mg a day, and a hangover breakfast (bacon, eggs, toast, a breakfast sandwich) can easily add another 1,000 mg or more. A single heavy day of salt isn't dangerous for a healthy person, but it's not a goal either.
- **Sugar adds up too.** Three sticks of the original formula is around 33 g of sugar, close to the amount in a can of soda.
- **Plain water still counts.** Once you've had one or two sticks, plain water is fine for the rest of the day. Your kidneys are very good at balancing salts once you've given them enough fluid.

### Who should be careful or skip it

Talk to your doctor before using Liquid I.V. or any high-sodium electrolyte drink regularly if you:

- Have high blood pressure or have been told to follow a low-salt diet
- Have kidney disease, where extra potassium and sodium can be hard to clear
- Have heart failure or have been told to limit fluids
- Take medicines that raise potassium, such as some blood pressure drugs (ACE inhibitors and ARBs) or potassium-sparing water pills
- Have diabetes and need to count the sugar (the sugar-free version may suit you better)

For everyone else, one or two sticks after a night out is a normal, reasonable use.

## Sugar-Free, Energy, and Sleep Versions After Drinking

The different Liquid I.V. lines behave differently the morning after.

**Sugar-Free.** Fine for rehydration, especially if you're limiting sugar. Some people find sugar alcohols and sweeteners like allulose upset their stomach in larger amounts, which matters if your gut is already unhappy. Start with one stick.

**Energy versions (with caffeine).** Caffeine can help a hangover headache for some people and is the reason coffee feels helpful the next morning. But it can also make shakiness, a racing heart, and anxiety worse, and it may nudge you to pee more. If you're already jittery or your heart is pounding, a non-caffeinated stick is the better choice. Never use caffeine to "sober up" during a night out. It makes you feel more alert without lowering your blood alcohol, which is how people end up making risky decisions like driving.

**Sleep versions.** These have contained melatonin and other calming ingredients. Combining a sleep aid with a lot of alcohol in your system isn't ideal, because both make you drowsy and alcohol already disrupts sleep. If you want to use one, wait until the alcohol has cleared, and check the label for the exact ingredients. When in doubt, a plain hydration stick before bed is the safer pick.

## Liquid I.V. Pros and Cons for Hangovers

Here's a fair summary.

**Pros**

- Real rehydration science (the sodium-glucose principle), not just flavoring
- More sodium than typical sports drinks, so it rehydrates better than Gatorade-style drinks
- Single-serve sticks are easy to carry in a bag or pack for a trip
- Tastes better than many medical rehydration products, so people actually drink it
- Widely available in grocery stores, pharmacies, and big-box stores

**Cons**

- Only addresses dehydration, which is one part of a hangover
- Costs noticeably more per serving than store-brand rehydration powders or plain water
- The original formula contains about 11 g of sugar per stick
- High sodium isn't a good fit for people on salt-restricted diets
- The vitamins added to it aren't what makes it work; most people aren't short on them after one night out
- Marketing language ("multiplier," "faster than water alone") can set expectations higher than a hangover will reward

If you already own it, use it. If you're choosing what to buy, a store-brand oral rehydration powder or Pedialyte will do much the same job, often for less. Coconut water is a gentler, lower-sodium option some people prefer; our [coconut water for hangovers](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) piece covers where it fits.

## A Simple Morning-After Plan That Includes Liquid I.V.

If you wake up hungover, here's a reasonable order of operations:

1. **Rehydrate gently.** Mix one stick of Liquid I.V. in 16 ounces of water and sip it over 20 to 30 minutes. If you didn't have one before bed, this is your main rehydration move.
2. **Eat something simple.** Toast, crackers, eggs, a banana, or oatmeal. Food helps your blood sugar and settles the stomach.
3. **Treat a headache carefully.** If you need a painkiller, take it with food and stick to the label dose. Avoid acetaminophen (Tylenol) if you're still drinking or drink heavily on a regular basis, because of the liver risk.
4. **Keep drinking plain water** through the day. You don't need more electrolyte sticks after the first one or two.
5. **Rest if you can.** Sleep repairs a lot of what alcohol took from you overnight.
6. **Skip the "hair of the dog."** More alcohol only postpones the hangover.

Our roundup of [the best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) compares Liquid I.V. with the other common options if you want to see the full field.

## When to See a Doctor

Most hangovers are miserable but harmless, and they clear within a day. Some symptoms are different and need real care.

> **Get medical help if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting repeatedly or see blood in your vomit, you have signs of serious dehydration (very little or no urine for 8 hours or more, dizziness or fainting when you stand, a fast heartbeat that won't settle, confusion), or you have chest pain, a severe headache unlike your usual ones, or trouble breathing. **Call 911 right away** if someone who's been drinking is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, having a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and an electrolyte drink is not the answer. Don't let them "sleep it off."
>
> If you notice shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart that shows up every time you go a day without drinking, that can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover. That's worth raising with a doctor plainly and soon, because withdrawal can be medically serious and is very treatable.

When fluid losses are large, especially from repeated vomiting, a clinic may give IV fluids. That's what "IV" actually means, and it's very different from a drink mix with "IV" in its brand name.

## Can You Prevent the Dehydration Part Entirely?

You can make it a lot smaller. The habits that help most are simple:

- **Eat a real meal before drinking.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers the details.
- **Alternate every drink with a glass of water.** It hydrates you and slows the pace, which matters more.
- **Set a drink limit before you go out**, and count drinks rather than guessing.
- **Choose lighter drinks.** Clear spirits with a non-sugary mixer tend to produce milder hangovers than dark liquors and sweet cocktails for many people.
- **Have water (or one electrolyte stick) before bed.**

The single most reliable way to have less of a hangover is to drink less alcohol. Everything else, Liquid I.V. included, is about trimming the edges. For a fuller playbook, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits Alongside Liquid I.V.

Since Liquid I.V. only handles the fluid side, some people pair it with a supplement aimed at a different part of the problem. The most studied option in that space is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree.

To be clear about the evidence: most DHM research is in animals and lab studies. In rats, DHM reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal and appeared to support how the body handles alcohol and its by-products. Human research is limited and early. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people, and it does not lower your blood alcohol or make drinking safer. It also doesn't replace water or electrolytes; it targets a different piece of the picture.

If you want to try it, people usually take it with water before bed after drinking, the same time you'd have a Liquid I.V. stick. Two options we've reviewed are [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a simple single-ingredient product at a lower cost per serving, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds L-cysteine and a few other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts and timing. As with any supplement, check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you take regular medicines.

## The Bottom Line

Liquid I.V. is a well-made rehydration drink that does what rehydration drinks do: it helps you replace water and salts faster than water alone. After a night out, that can ease thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness, and a dehydration headache. It does not clear acetaldehyde, calm inflammation, repair your sleep, or settle an irritated stomach, which is why a hangover usually lingers even when you're well hydrated.

Use one stick before bed and one in the morning, sip it slowly, eat something, and drink plain water the rest of the day. Skip it or talk to a doctor if you're on a low-salt diet or have kidney or heart problems. And if you can't keep fluids down or someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, get medical help instead of reaching for another drink mix.

faq.question: Does Liquid I.V. help with a hangover?
faq.answer: Partly. Liquid I.V. is a sodium-and-sugar rehydration mix, so it helps with the dehydration part of a hangover: thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness, and a dehydration headache. It does nothing about acetaldehyde, inflammation, poor sleep, or stomach irritation, which drive most hangover misery. There is no good evidence that it prevents or cures a hangover on its own.

faq.question: Should I take Liquid I.V. before or after drinking?
faq.answer: Before bed after drinking and the next morning are the most useful times. A stick before bed gives your body hours to absorb fluid while alcohol is still making you pee. Having one before you go out starts you well hydrated but doesn't stop alcohol's effect on your kidneys. Don't mix it into alcoholic drinks.

faq.question: How many Liquid I.V. sticks can I have in a day?
faq.answer: One or two is enough for a hangover, such as one before bed and one in the morning. Check your package's guidance and don't exceed it. Each original stick has roughly 500 mg of sodium and about 11 g of sugar, so several sticks plus a salty breakfast adds up fast. After that, plain water is fine.

faq.question: Is Liquid I.V. better than Pedialyte for a hangover?
faq.answer: They do much the same job. Both use the sodium-glucose principle to rehydrate faster than water, and their sodium levels are in a similar range. Pedialyte is a little closer to a medical rehydration formula, while Liquid I.V. comes in portable sticks many people find tastier. Pick whichever you'll actually drink, or a cheaper store-brand rehydration powder.

faq.question: Is Liquid I.V. better than Gatorade for a hangover?
faq.answer: For rehydration, generally yes. Regular sports drinks have much less sodium and more sugar per serving, so they're weaker at replacing the fluid and salt lost after drinking. Neither one addresses the non-dehydration causes of a hangover.

faq.question: Can I use the caffeinated or sleep versions of Liquid I.V. after drinking?
faq.answer: Be cautious. Caffeine can help some hangover headaches but may worsen shakiness, a racing heart, and anxiety. Sleep versions have contained melatonin, and combining sleep aids with alcohol still in your system isn't ideal. A plain, non-caffeinated hydration stick is the safer choice the night of and the morning after.

faq.question: Who should avoid Liquid I.V.?
faq.answer: Talk to a doctor first if you have high blood pressure or follow a low-salt diet, have kidney disease or heart failure, take medicines that raise potassium (such as some blood pressure drugs or potassium-sparing water pills), or need to count sugar for diabetes. For healthy adults, one or two sticks after a night out is a normal use.

faq.question: When is a hangover a reason to see a doctor instead of drinking electrolytes?
faq.answer: Get help if you can't keep fluids down for several hours, are vomiting repeatedly or see blood, have very little urine, feel faint when standing, or are confused. Call 911 if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, having a seizure, or has cold, pale, or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning.
